turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi. Thanks for making the time today. I'm Daniel, and I led the product team for our analytics platform here at Northwind. How are you doing?

turns.speaker: you
turns.text: Doing well, thanks Daniel. I've been looking forward to this. I actually spent some time with your dashboard product this weekend.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Oh, great. Let's start with a quick walkthrough of your background.

turns.speaker: you
turns.text: Sure. I'm a product manager at a mid-size logistics software company, where I own our routing and dispatch product. Over the last three years I've grown it from about 2 million to 11 million dollars in annual revenue. Before that I was a data analyst, which is why analytics products are close to my heart.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a time you had to make a tough prioritization call.

turns.speaker: you
turns.text: Last year our largest customer asked for a custom reporting feature. While our data showed that 40% of new users were dropping off during onboarding, and we only had one team for the quarter, I pulled the churn and expansion numbers, showed that fixing onboarding was worth roughly three times the revenue of the custom feature, and proposed a lightweight export as a stopgap for the big customer. We shipped the onboarding redesign in eight weeks. Activation went from 60 to 78%, and the customer renewed anyway.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's a great example. How did the customer react to hearing no?

turns.speaker: you
turns.text: I called their VP myself before they heard it anywhere else. Explained the trade-off. And gave them a firm date for the export. Being direct early actually built trust.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you work with engineering when estimates slip?

turns.speaker: you
turns.text: I treat an estimate as a hypothesis. When something slips, I first ask the team what we learned. If the date matters to customers, I cut scope instead of moving the date. On my current team we define a must-have slice for every project up front, so those conversations take 10 minutes instead of a week.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What would you want to accomplish in your first 90 days here?

turns.speaker: you
turns.text: In the first month, I'd listen. Talk to at least 20 customers and sit in on sales calls. In the second month, I'd pick one metric with the team, probably activation for the new self-serve tier. In the third month, I'd ship a first improvement against it and set up a weekly review so we can see whether it's working.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: I love that. Honestly, that's very close to what we need. Our self-serve tier launched in the spring, and activation is our biggest open question. The team is six engineers and a designer, and you'd report to me. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: you
turns.text: Two questions. What does success look like for this role after one year? And what's the biggest disagreement the team has right now about the roadmap?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Great questions. Success is activation above 70% and a clear self-serve roadmap. The biggest debate is whether to build integrations or improve the core dashboards, and I'd love your take on that in the next round. We're running a bit over, but this was a really good conversation. Our recruiter will reach out tomorrow to set up the on-site with our engineering-led and our CEO.

turns.speaker: you
turns.text: Thank you, Daniel. I really enjoyed this, and I'm excited about the activation problem. Talk soon.

plan.headline: This was a strong hiring-manager round, and Daniel has already lined up an on-site with the engineering lead and CEO, so your single most important move is to arrive with a structured, product-grounded view on integrations vs. core dashboards, tied to self-serve activation.

next_round_prep.topic: Integrations vs. core dashboards roadmap debate
next_round_prep.why: Daniel told you directly this is the team's biggest disagreement and that he wants your view in the next round. Expect him or the CEO to ask it outright.

evidence.quote: The biggest debate is whether to build integrations or improve the core dashboards, and I'd love your take on that in the next round.

next_round_prep.how_to_prepare: Lead with how you would decide, not what you would pick. Reuse the method from your onboarding story: you pulled churn and expansion numbers and showed onboarding was worth roughly three times the revenue of the custom feature. Apply the same lens here. Ask which option moves self-serve activation, where trial users drop off, which integrations prospects and churned users ask for, and the engineering cost for a team of six. Close with a tentative lean and a cheap test before committing. Your lightweight-export stopgap is a good model for a small first test. Have a 90-second spoken version and a longer version ready.
likely_questions: So, integrations or core dashboards: what would you do and why?
What data would you need before you'd commit to one direction?
How would you test this cheaply with only six engineers?

next_round_prep.why: Daniel named activation above 70% as the one-year success measure and called activation their biggest open question. You mentioned using the product but never turned it into an insight.

evidence.quote: Success is activation above 70% and a clear self-serve roadmap.

next_round_prep.how_to_prepare: Connect your real result to their target. Your data showed 40% of new users dropping off in onboarding, and after the redesign activation went from 60 to 78%. Then bring in what you saw in their dashboard product this weekend. Write down two or three specific observations and form an early hypothesis about where self-serve users stall. Use one of them to sharpen month two of your 90-day plan. Be ready to define activation, for example what 'first value' means for a dashboard user.
likely_questions: How would you define activation for our self-serve tier?
You said you used the product. What did you notice, and what would you look at first?
How would you get activation above 70%, and how fast is realistic?

next_round_prep.topic: Working with the engineering lead day to day
next_round_prep.why: The on-site includes the engineering lead, and the report found your answer on slipping estimates described a philosophy without a specific example. That is exactly what an engineering lead will press on.

evidence.quote: Our recruiter will reach out tomorrow to set up the on-site with our engineering-led and our CEO.

next_round_prep.how_to_prepare: An engineering lead will want to know how you'll treat their team day to day. Keep your principles: an estimate is a hypothesis, ask what you learned first, and cut scope rather than move dates that matter to customers. But attach one real moment from your current team where you used the must-have slice, with what was cut and what shipped. Only use an instance that actually happened, such as something from the eight-week onboarding redesign if it fits. Also prepare how you'd involve engineers in the integrations-vs-dashboards decision and how you'd handle technical debt requests.
likely_questions: Tell me about a specific time an estimate slipped. What happened?
How do you decide between paying down tech debt and shipping features?
How would you involve engineering in deciding integrations vs. dashboards?

next_round_prep.topic: CEO conversation: why Northwind and business judgment
next_round_prep.why: You'll meet the CEO next, and the report found your background answer never linked to Northwind or explained why this role now.

evidence.quote: Before that I was a data analyst, which is why analytics products are close to my heart.

next_round_prep.how_to_prepare: A CEO will want the business story and your motivation. Tighten your background into a version that ends with Northwind. Grew routing and dispatch from about $2M to $11M in three years. Data-analyst roots, which is why analytics products appeal to you. Why Northwind's self-serve analytics, and why now. Weave in your weekend product exploration. Also prepare the business side of your prioritization story: why trading a big customer's request for onboarding was the right revenue call, and how that customer renewed.
likely_questions: How did you grow your product from $2M to $11M?
How would you balance big-customer requests against self-serve growth?

next_round_prep.why: Daniel's follow-up asked about the customer's reaction, and you answered with your own actions. With integrations on the table, saying no to customers and sales is likely to come up again.

evidence.quote: That's a great example. How did the customer react to hearing no?

next_round_prep.how_to_prepare: Your answer covered what you did: you called their VP, explained the trade-off and gave a firm export date. It didn't say how the customer responded in the moment. Recall what the VP actually said or did and have that ready, if you remember it. Also prepare whether sales or leadership pushed back internally, and how you handled them.
likely_questions: How did the customer respond when you told them no?
Did anyone internally push back on not building the custom feature?
How would you handle a large customer demanding an integration we haven't prioritized?

practice_plan.from_coaching: Arrive at the on-site with a view on integrations vs. dashboards
practice_plan.drill: In 15 minutes, draft a one-page take on integrations vs. core dashboards: decision criteria (activation impact, churn reasons, competitive gaps, engineering cost), the data you'd want, a tentative lean and one cheap test. Then rehearse a 90-second spoken version aloud three times, starting with how you'd decide.

practice_plan.from_coaching: Turn your product homework into a specific insight
practice_plan.drill: Spend 10 minutes in Northwind's dashboard product and note three specific observations. Turn each into 'When I used your product, I noticed X, which makes me think Y about activation.' Say each aloud until it takes under 20 seconds, then add one to month two of your 90-day plan.

practice_plan.from_coaching: Back process answers with one specific story
practice_plan.drill: Pick three likely process questions: estimates slipping, a stakeholder disagreement, and what to cut. For each, write one sentence of principle plus three sentences of a real example ending in a measurable outcome. Say each aloud and time it to under 60 seconds.

practice_plan.from_coaching: Turn your product homework into a specific insight
practice_plan.drill: Rewrite your background walkthrough so it ends with why Northwind and why now, and mentions your weekend product exploration. Rehearse it aloud in under 60 seconds, twice, as if the CEO had just asked.

practice_plan.from_coaching: Arrive at the on-site with a view on integrations vs. dashboards
practice_plan.drill: Have a friend or a notes file give you three short interviewer answers (e.g. 'success is activation above 70%'). After each, practise a two-sentence reaction with a first hypothesis before moving on.
